content.text:
I submitted an inverse-volatility-weighted portfolio of all 94 `tsmom_<IND>_21` and `tsmom_<IND>_126` signals. These are the 21-day and 126-day trend-following signals on each hedged industry. It scored a Sharpe ratio of 0.12 in training (1970–1999) and 0.41 in validation (2000–2012).

I made every choice using the training data only and ran `bt.backtest` just once, on the final portfolio. I could have used up to 5,000 backtest calls to search for weights with a higher validation Sharpe. I didn't, because tuning on the validation period would make its Sharpe an overfit number and no longer a fair test.

The training data showed these signals are mostly noise:
- **Optimised weights didn't hold up.** I fitted weights on 1970–1989 and tested them on 1990–1999. Mean-variance weights scored about 3–4.6 on the years they were fitted to and about −0.5 on the later years.
- **Past winners didn't repeat.** Individual signals' Sharpe ratios in the first part of training had a correlation of −0.10 with their Sharpe ratios in the later years.
- **Only two families were positive throughout.** Of the nine signal families, only the 21-day and 126-day trend signals had a positive Sharpe in both the early and late training years. They were also positive in four of the six five-year blocks, so I combined just those two with simple equal-risk weights.
